note: Six independently inspected historical, environmental, and primary-document additions for editorial integration. This is a supplement, not a replacement profile. Current tribal sources should lead identity and government; these works have different geographic and historical scopes. No main site data was altered.

sources.title: The Classification and Distribution of the Pit River Indian Tribes of California
sources.author: C. Hart Merriam
sources.annotation: Published December 31, 1926, pp. 1–52. Read printed pp. 1–5, 12–14, 24–26, and selected name entries on pp. 41–47 in the full scan. Merriam acknowledges named Indigenous contributors and records variable names and contrasting environments. His narrower Fall River use of A-choo-mah-we and period classification require context; the map and taxonomy do not establish present jurisdiction or modern band membership. His salvage-era assumptions should not be repeated as statements about contemporary people.

sources.title: PG&E Land Transfers Final Mitigated Negative Declaration: Section 2-V, Cultural Resources
sources.publisher: California Public Utilities Commission / Environmental Science Associates
sources.annotation: Read the HTML sections on ethnographic and archaeological background, historical background, McArthur Swamp, surveys, and regulatory setting. This early-2000s project review summarizes settlement, forced removal, wetland engineering, and consultation. It concerns particular Shasta County parcels, not all Pit River territory. Its language-family terminology and archaeological chronology need independent qualification. Its account of consultation does not demonstrate tribal consent or establish current law or a final transfer outcome.

sources.title: Ahjumawi Lava Springs State Park
sources.annotation: Four-page public brochure, copyright 2012, revised 2016; read PDF pp. 2–3 on Ajumawi history, stone fish traps, springs, and habitat. Its local focus is the Ajumawi band and the Fall River basin. It describes harvest restraint and protection of spawning fish as part of fishery management. This agency interpretation should not be generalized to every Achumawi-speaking community, and its dated visitor advice is not a current travel guide.

sources.title: Traders and Raiders: Aspects of Trans-Basin and California-Plateau Commerce, 1800–1830
sources.publisher: Journal of California and Great Basin Anthropology 3(1), pp. 127–137 / UC eScholarship
sources.author: Thomas N. Layton
sources.annotation: 1981 article; closely read printed pp. 127–131 and checked the later discussion on pp. 134–135. Layton combines earlier ethnography and travel accounts to examine exchange, horses, and captive-taking across a large region. He identifies uneven evidence and explicitly states that the predicted settlement changes had not been investigated in Pit River territory. His Surprise Valley archaeological examples cannot serve as direct evidence of an Achumawi settlement shift.

sources.title: The Achumawi Life-Force
sources.publisher: Journal of California Anthropology 2(1), pp. 60–63 / UC eScholarship
sources.author: Jaime de Angulo; translated by Annette Boushey
sources.annotation: Read all four pages of the 1975 English translation, excerpted from a 1928 French essay. De Angulo presents reported conversations alongside his own speculative theories and period stereotypes. This is evidence of a mediated historical encounter, not a complete or community-approved account of present belief. The profile proposal discusses relationships and representation without reproducing ritual wording, offerings, or instructions contained in the essay.

sources.title: Comments of the Pit River Tribe on CPUC Applications 00-05-029 and 00-05-030
sources.publisher: California Indian Legal Services, on behalf of the Pit River Tribe; hosted by California Public Utilities Commission
sources.author: Michael P. Acosta, attorney for the Pit River Tribe
sources.annotation: December 10, 2001, four-page signed letter; all pages visually inspected. Read especially comments 2–4 and 6–7 on transfer alternatives, consultation, tribal authority over cultural resources, and the Ajumawi band's relationship to the Tribe. These are the Tribe's legal arguments at that time, rather than adjudicated findings or the agency's position. It is a distinct primary submission, not a second copy of the environmental review.

proposedParagraphs.title: Names need a date, speaker, and scale
proposedParagraphs.text: Merriam's 1926 study records names whose forms vary with speaker and context. His account acknowledges Indigenous contributors, including Istet Woiche and people from several other communities. It also uses A-choo-mah-we for a particular Fall River community, alongside a broader classification of related peoples. This helps explain why historical spellings cannot simply be treated as interchangeable labels for a language, every band, and today's government. Merriam describes marked differences between forested western country and the drier eastern country. His publication offers evidence about an earlier research encounter and geographic diversity; its categories and map should be read beside current tribal accounts rather than used to settle present boundaries.

proposedParagraphs.title: Ajumawi water knowledge in the Fall River basin
proposedParagraphs.text: California State Parks' public brochure locates Ajumawi history in the spring-fed waters of the Fall River basin. It describes stone fish traps that guided fish through channels and shallow water, connecting engineering with knowledge of springs and spawning behavior. The brochure also describes limits on harvesting and protection of spawning fish. These are accounts of a managed fishery rather than a landscape untouched by people. The same publication discusses volcanic groundwater and threats to native aquatic habitat. Its account concerns this particular Ajumawi landscape; it should not become a single subsistence description for all Achumawi-speaking communities across contrasting environments.

proposedParagraphs.title: Trade networks, captivity, and the limits of inference
proposedParagraphs.text: Layton's 1981 article places Pit River people within wider networks linking the California Plateau, Great Basin, and Columbia River. His synthesis describes exchange as well as raids and the trafficking of captives, drawing on older ethnographic and travel accounts. Those relationships varied across communities and time; they do not justify portraying neighboring peoples as permanent enemies. Layton proposes that mounted raiding could have encouraged more defensible settlements. Crucially, he says the relevant settlement research had not been conducted in Pit River territory. His archaeological comparisons from Surprise Valley are therefore a regional hypothesis to investigate, not proof that every Achumawi community followed the same sequence.

proposedParagraphs.title: Violence, removal, and an altered wetland landscape
proposedParagraphs.text: The CPUC's project-specific cultural review connects nineteenth-century settlement around Fall River with retaliatory killing, Fort Crook, and forced removal to Round Valley in 1859. It also describes people returning afterward. This compressed agency history should be expanded with tribal accounts rather than treated as the experience of every family. The review traces another transformation through drainage of Big Lake, levee construction, ranching, and hydroelectric development. These changes help explain why the current wetland landscape cannot stand in for conditions before colonization. Its archaeological summaries concern surveyed project parcels, with acknowledged gaps; they cannot establish a single starting date for all Pit River history.

proposedParagraphs.title: Reading an early ethnographic account critically
proposedParagraphs.text: De Angulo's essay preserves reported conversations about life and relationships among people, water, trees, and rocks. The available English text appeared in 1975 as a translation of part of a 1928 French essay. Speakers' words therefore reach readers through the author's selection and a later translation, alongside his speculative theories and stereotypes. It can support careful study of how knowledge was represented in an earlier encounter. It should not define a uniform present-day belief system or authorize reproducing ceremonial instructions.

proposedParagraphs.title: A primary tribal argument about land and cultural authority
proposedParagraphs.text: A December 2001 letter submitted by California Indian Legal Services for the Pit River Tribe challenges proposed Shasta County land transfers. It argues that the Tribe should have been considered as a land recipient and that replacing existing protections would weaken cultural-resource care. It also objects to concentrating decisions in a nontribal archaeologist and stresses tribal knowledge of historical and intangible significance. Comment 7 specifically corrects the proposed measure's description of the Ajumawi band's relationship to the Pit River Tribe. The letter records the Tribe's position in that proceeding; it is not a finding that every legal claim was upheld or evidence of today's ownership.

integrationNotes: These six sources are additional to the tribal constitution, tribal history, language work, court records, and monument materials handled by the parent researcher. Deduplicate by work, not merely URL.

Merriam's historical hierarchy and nine-versus-two grouping are not a substitute for current constitutional band names. Modern Ajumawi/Atsugewi governance and language relationships need current tribal and specialist sources.
The CPUC review and the CILS letter are distinct works with different authors and evidentiary functions. They should never be collapsed into an implication that the Tribe agreed with the review.
The translated de Angulo essay is optional historical-representation context. Retain its caveats and do not mine it for ceremonial directions or generalize its authorial claims to all people today.

No historic village coordinates, burial locations, ceremonial formulae, or detailed restricted knowledge are reproduced. Public archive access alone is not evidence of community permission for unrestricted reuse.
The six paragraphs provide modular research prose, not a demand for six additional sections. Integrate into a coherent profile and cite all retained sources substantively.
researchGaps: More community-authored histories from different Achumawi-speaking bands are needed to balance early ethnography and agency summaries.

The suggested link between mounted raiding and settlement change remains untested for Pit River territory within the Layton passages reviewed; direct, appropriately shareable archaeological evidence would be required.
The 2001 land-transfer dispute is historical. Current ownership, the final administrative outcome, and later cultural-resource agreements were not established by this supplement.
Current fishery work and the role of Ajumawi experts in present restoration should be documented from community-approved sources before describing contemporary management.
